extracted.intended_audience: general public; students or practitioners seeking a summary of the legal concept of jury tampering (esp. UK/Ireland/US)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize the legal definition, acts that constitute jury tampering, jurisdictional remedies (non‑jury trials, Special Criminal Court), and illustrative cases across the UK, Ireland, and the United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of jury tampering
rubrics_metrics.description: “Jury tampering is the crime of unduly attempting to influence the composition or decisions of a jury during the course of a trial.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page explains this includes attempts to influence selection (discrediting potential jurors), influencing jurors once selected (bribery, intimidation), or making unauthorized contact to introduce prohibited outside information and cause a mistrial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrediting potential jurors to prevent selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting to discredit potential jurors so they will not be selected for duty is an act that can constitute jury tampering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as one means by which the crime can be perpetrated (i.e., manipulating jury composition through exclusion of particular jurors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bribery or intimidation of selected jurors
rubrics_metrics.description: Bribing or intimidating jurors after they are selected to induce them to act in a certain manner on duty is jury tampering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and historic convictions (e.g., George Pape selling his vote in the Gotti trial) illustrate bribery leading to convictions and prison sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized contact and introducing outside information
rubrics_metrics.description: Making unauthorized contact with jurors for the purpose of introducing prohibited outside information and then arguing for a mistrial constitutes jury tampering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights introducing outside information as a ground for charging tampering and for seeking retrial or other remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communications that encourage jurors to ignore judge instructions (U.S. example)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States, people have been charged with jury tampering for handing out pamphlets and flyers indicating jurors have certain rights and obligations, including an obligation to 'vote their conscience' notwithstanding the instructions they are given by the judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows that even seemingly informational communications can be charged as tampering if they encourage jurors to disregard judicial directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of non‑jury trial where danger of jury tampering exists (UK: Criminal Justice Act 2003)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Criminal Justice Act 2003 allows for non‑jury trials when there is danger of jury tampering, or where jury tampering has taken place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites a landmark Court of Appeal decision invoking Section 44 to permit a criminal trial without a jury after multiple juries failed to reach verdicts or were discharged (Heathrow armed robbery case). It also references Diplock Courts (Northern Ireland) as precedent for non‑jury courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Special Criminal Court in Ireland when ordinary courts are inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: In Ireland, the Special Criminal Court (a three‑judge, juryless court) is used where 'ordinary courts are inadequate to secure the effective administration of justice'; it was established to handle cases where the risk of jury intimidation was high.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes constitutional allowance and historical justification (1972 establishment to handle paramilitary cases during the Troubles), and later use for high‑risk gang-related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical remedies and consequences following tampering (retrial, non‑jury trial, convictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When jury tampering is alleged or proven, remedies can include retrial before a judge sitting alone, or criminal prosecution/conviction of those who tampered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative cases: repeated discharged juries led to a judge-alone trial ending in convictions (Heathrow case); attempts to bribe jurors in Northern Ireland led to retrial before a judge alone; named individuals (e.g., Gil Dozier, Jimmy Hoffa, William Wallace Barron) convicted of jury tampering demonstrate enforcement outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Related offences and doctrinal distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Jury tampering is related to but distinct from other offences such as contempt of court, embracery, obstruction of justice, and witness tampering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists these related concepts to clarify classification and to point readers to overlapping legal doctrines and remedies.
